title: Web Chat Client
prompt: Design the browser client for a messaging app with one-to-one and group chats. Messages should appear instantly, survive a flaky connection, and unread counts should stay correct.

clarify.q: One-to-one only, or groups too? How big can a group get?
clarify.why: Big groups (500+ members) mean bursts of messages, so we batch renders. They also make per-member read receipts expensive to show.

clarify.q: Must sending work while offline, with messages going out later?
clarify.why: Yes means a durable outbox in IndexedDB and idempotent sends. No means a simple 'failed, tap to retry' state.

clarify.q: Do we keep history on the device for instant open and offline reading?
clarify.why: It decides whether IndexedDB is a cache of recent messages or the main local database, and how we sync on start.

clarify.q: Is the app often open in several tabs at once?
clarify.why: Several tabs means unread counts and read state must agree across tabs, and we probably want one socket, not one per tab.

clarify.q: Which features beyond text: typing indicators, read receipts, reactions, attachments, edits?
clarify.why: Each adds event types to the protocol. Edits and reactions mean a message changes after it arrives, so the store must update in place.
E2EE moves key management and decryption into the client, often into a worker, and makes server-side search impossible. It is a different design.

functional: List conversations sorted by latest activity, each with an unread count and a preview.
Send a message that appears at once with a 'sending' state, then 'sent' when the server confirms.
Receive messages live while the conversation is open or in the background.
Queue messages written while offline and send them in order when back online.
Scroll up to load older history; open at the first unread message.
Keep unread counts and read state in sync across open tabs, and show the total in the tab title.
nonFunctional: A sent message appears in the list within 1 frame (16.7 ms) of pressing Enter.
Messages in a conversation always show in server order; no duplicates, even after reconnects and retries.
No message typed by the user is ever lost, including across a page reload while offline.
Reconnect within ~1 s after a short blip; spread reconnects so a server restart doesn't cause a thundering herd.
Smooth scroll in a conversation with thousands of loaded messages on a mid-range laptop and phone.
Accessible: new messages announced politely, full keyboard use, focus kept in the composer.
outOfScope: The server side: message storage, fan-out, presence service (the backend chat-system problem).

assumptions: Active user is in 50 conversations; receives ~200 messages per hour, peaks of 20 messages/s in busy groups
One message is ~300 bytes of JSON (ids, seq, author, text, timestamps)
1 M users connected at once; a desktop user has 2 tabs open on average
Proxies drop idle sockets after ~60 s
A message bubble is ~25 DOM nodes

steps.label: Render pressure in a busy group
steps.math: 20 messages/s arriving; one render each = 20 renders/s, each touching the list
steps.result: Batch: apply all frames received in one animation frame as one store update

steps.label: Sockets: per tab vs one per browser
steps.math: 1 M users × 2 tabs = 2 M sockets; with one leader tab per browser = 1 M
steps.result: Half the server connections, and one source of truth per browser

steps.label: Reconnect storm after a server deploy
steps.math: 1 M clients reconnecting in ~1 s = 1 M handshakes/s. Full jitter over 0–30 s: 1 M ÷ 30 s

steps.label: Backoff schedule
steps.math: Base 1 s, doubling, cap 30 s: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 30… Sum before hitting the cap = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16
steps.result: ≈ 31 s of retries before the cap; each delay is a random value between 0 and that ceiling

steps.label: Catch-up after being offline
steps.math: 10 min: 200/h × 1/6 h ≈ 33 messages × 300 B ≈ 10 KB. A weekend: 48 h × 200/h ≈ 9 600 messages × 300 B ≈ 2.9 MB
steps.result: Short gaps: replay events. Long gaps: fetch the latest 50 per conversation and load the rest on scroll

steps.label: DOM in a long conversation
steps.math: 5 000 loaded messages × 25 nodes = 125 000 nodes. Windowed: ~40 bubbles × 25

steps.label: Detecting a dead socket
steps.math: App ping every 25 s (below the 60 s idle timeout) + 10 s pong timeout
steps.result: Dead connection found within ~35 s worst case; online and visibility events check sooner

estimates.takeaway: Bandwidth is tiny: messages are 300 bytes. The hard parts are correctness under reconnects (ordering, dedupe, no lost sends) and coordination (jittered backoff so 1 M clients don't return in the same second, one socket per browser rather than per tab). Long offline gaps should not be replayed message by message. Batch incoming messages per frame and virtualise long histories.

api.body: ConversationView { conversationId, initialAnchor: 'first-unread' | 'latest' }; Composer { conversationId, onSend(text, attachments), maxLength = 4000 }
api.returns: Conversation list, message list (role log) and composer
api.note: Components read from the store by id; only the Composer emits user intents. Draft text is saved per conversation.

api.body: { type: 'send', clientId, conversationId, body } · { type: 'read', conversationId, seq } · { type: 'typing', conversationId } · { type: 'ping' }
api.returns: Server replies with ack or error per clientId
api.note: clientId is a UUID made in the browser before the message is stored in the outbox. The server dedupes on (sender, clientId).

api.body: { type: 'ack', clientId, id, seq, ts } · { type: 'message', message } · { type: 'read', conversationId, userId, seq } · { type: 'pong' } · close code 4401 = token expired
api.returns: Every event carries a global eventCursor for catch-up
api.note: seq is a per-conversation counter assigned by the server; it defines display order.

api.returns: 200 { events: [...], nextCursor, hasMore } or 409 { reset: true } if the cursor is too old
api.note: Replays what was missed. A 409 means 'too far behind', so the client refetches conversations and the latest page of each open one.
Cursor is the seq number itself: stable, because history never reorders.

api.returns: 200 { items: [{ id, title, lastSeq, lastReadSeq, preview, updatedAt }], nextCursor }
api.note: Unread count = lastSeq − lastReadSeq, computed on the client.

entities.name: conversations.byId
entities.why: Unread count is derived from two numbers, so it can never drift from a separate counter.

entities.name: messages[conversationId]
entities.why: Keying by clientId means the optimistic copy and the server echo land on the same entry, so no duplicate.

entities.name: outbox
entities.why: Durable across reloads and crashes. Written before the message is shown as 'sending', so nothing typed is lost.

entities.name: connection
entities.store: Leader tab memory, broadcast to other tabs
entities.why: An explicit state machine is what makes reconnect logic testable.

data.note: The URL holds only the open conversation: /c/:conversationId, plus an optional ?m=messageId for deep links to a message. Drafts, outbox and recent history live in IndexedDB, written from a small data layer that every tab shares. Display order is seq, never the client clock, because device clocks are wrong. Pending messages have no seq yet and sit after all confirmed ones, in their createdAt order.

hld.summary:
One tab per browser is elected leader with the Web Locks API. The leader owns the WebSocket, the reconnect state machine and the outbox flush. Every tab, leader included, talks to it over a BroadcastChannel: tabs post 'send' and 'read' intents, and the leader posts incoming events and connection state. If the leader tab closes, its lock is released and another tab takes over and reconnects.

Each tab has its own normalised store fed by those events, plus IndexedDB as the shared durable layer (recent messages, drafts, outbox, eventCursor). The UI is a conversation list, a virtualised message list that sticks to the bottom, and a composer. Sending writes to the outbox first, shows the message optimistically, then the leader sends it. The server ack carries the real id and seq, and the message moves into place.

diagram.title: Tabs, leader and data flow
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Tab1[Leader tab]
    WS[Socket manager and state machine]
    OB[Outbox flusher]
    UI1[Store and UI]
  end
  subgraph Tab2[Follower tab]
    UI2[Store and UI]
  end
  BC((BroadcastChannel))
  IDB[("IndexedDB: messages, outbox, cursor")]
  SRV[Chat server]
  WS <-->|frames| SRV
  WS -->|events| BC
  BC --> UI1
  BC --> UI2
  UI2 -->|send and read intents| BC
  BC --> OB
  OB --> WS
  UI1 --> IDB
  OB --> IDB

flows.title: Sending a message
steps: Composer makes clientId, writes { clientId, body, status: queued } to the outbox, and adds a pending message to the store in the same tick.
Bubble appears at the bottom with a clock icon; the screen reader is not interrupted.
Leader picks it up and sends { type: send, clientId } if the socket is open.
Server stores it (deduping by clientId) and replies ack { clientId, id, seq }.
Store moves the message from pending to its seq position; outbox row is deleted; tick icon shows.
No ack in 10 s: mark it for resend on the next open socket; the server dedupe makes this safe.

flows.title: Reconnecting after a blip
steps: Socket closes or a pong is missed; state goes open → backoff with attempt 1.
Wait a random 0–1 s, then connecting; if the browser is offline, wait for the online event instead.
On open, call /v1/sync?since=eventCursor and apply missed events in order.
Flush the outbox in createdAt order per conversation.
Broadcast state open; banners in all tabs disappear.

flows.title: Reading in one tab clears unread everywhere
steps: Conversation is open, tab is visible and focused, and the newest message is on screen.
Tab sets lastReadSeq locally and posts a read intent on the BroadcastChannel.
Other tabs update their store; their badges and document titles drop at once.
Leader sends { type: read, seq } (throttled to one per 2 s per conversation); the server echoes to the user's other devices.

deepDives.title: Socket lifecycle and the reconnect state machine
deepDives.problem: Sockets die silently: laptops sleep, phones switch from Wi-Fi to cellular, proxies drop idle connections, and a server deploy disconnects everybody at once. Ad-hoc onclose = () => connect() code creates loops of instant retries, duplicate sockets, and herds of a million clients reconnecting in the same second.

options.name: Raw WebSocket with an explicit state machine
options.how: States idle, connecting, open, backoff, offline, auth. Exponential backoff with full jitter (random 0 to min(30 s, 1 s × 2^attempt)), app-level ping every 25 s, reset attempt after 30 s of stable connection.
pros: Full control; each transition is unit-testable
cons: You write and maintain the edge cases yourself

options.name: A realtime library (Socket.IO style)
options.how: Library handles reconnect, heartbeats and transport fallback.
cons: Ties the server to the library's protocol
Its ordering and dedupe guarantees still aren't yours

options.name: SSE for receiving plus HTTP POST for sending
options.how: EventSource streams events with Last-Event-ID; sends go over normal requests.
pros: Browser reconnects SSE and resends Last-Event-ID for you
cons: One-way: typing indicators and acks need extra requests
Per-domain connection limits on HTTP/1.1

deepDives.choice: Raw WebSocket with an explicit state machine, because ordering, dedupe and sync are ours anyway. Rules: never two sockets (the state machine owns the only reference); offline state waits for the online event instead of burning retries; close code 4401 goes to auth, refreshes the token, then reconnects without backoff; visibilitychange to visible and online both trigger an immediate ping. Show 'Reconnecting in 4 s · Retry now' in the UI. If corporate proxies blocked WebSockets for many customers, I would add SSE as a fallback transport.

diagram.title: Connection state machine
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  IDLE[idle] -->|start| CONN[connecting]
  CONN -->|socket open| OPEN[open]
  CONN -->|error| BACK["backoff (jittered wait)"]
  OPEN -->|close or missed pong| BACK
  BACK -->|timer fires| CONN
  BACK -->|browser offline| OFF[offline]
  OFF -->|online event| CONN
  OPEN -->|close code 4401| AUTH[refresh token]
  AUTH -->|new token| CONN
  OPEN -->|"stable 30 s: attempt = 0"| OPEN

deepDives.title: Ordering and dedupe
deepDives.problem: Messages can arrive twice (resent after a lost ack, replayed by sync), out of order (sync and live frames overlap), or with gaps (a frame lost during a reconnect). Client clocks are wrong by minutes. The UI must show one copy of each message in one agreed order.

options.name: Sort by client timestamp
options.how: Each client stamps createdAt; display sorts by it.
cons: Clock skew reorders conversations
Ties and duplicates are unresolved

options.name: Server per-conversation seq plus client ids
options.how: Server assigns seq 1, 2, 3… per conversation. Client keys messages by clientId (own messages) or id (others), sorts by seq, and tracks the highest contiguous seq to detect gaps.
pros: One total order everybody agrees on
Gaps are detectable: seq 41 then 43 means 42 is missing
cons: Needs a sequencer per conversation on the server
Pending messages have no seq until acked

options.name: Hybrid logical clocks
options.how: Order by (time, counter, node) tuples generated by each client.
cons: Complex; order can still surprise users
Overkill when a server sees every message

deepDives.choice: Server seq plus client ids. Insert by seq with a binary search, not a full sort. On a gap, wait 2 s for the missing frame, then fetch ?afterSeq=41&limit=50. Pending messages render after confirmed ones; when an ack arrives, the bubble moves to its seq slot, which is almost always the bottom. Use clientId as the React key from the start so the bubble doesn't remount when it gets its server id. A peer-to-peer or E2EE design with no trusted server would push me toward logical clocks.

deepDives.title: Offline outbox in IndexedDB
deepDives.problem: The user writes three messages on the subway, closes the laptop, and opens it at home. All three must send, once each, in order. Memory-only queues lose them on reload; naive retries send them twice.

options.name: In-memory queue
options.how: Array of pending sends, flushed on reconnect.
cons: Lost on reload, crash or tab close
Different per tab

options.name: IndexedDB outbox, flushed by the leader tab
options.how: Write before showing as sending; leader flushes oldest-first per conversation on open; delete on ack; server dedupes by clientId.
cons: Async writes add ~1–5 ms; must keep the optimistic UI independent of the write finishing
Needs schema versioning for upgrades

options.name: Service worker with Background Sync
options.how: Queue requests in the service worker; the browser replays them when connectivity returns, even if the tab is closed.
pros: Sends even after the tab closes
cons: Background Sync is Chromium-only
Needs the HTTP send endpoint, not the socket

deepDives.choice: IndexedDB outbox flushed by the leader, with Background Sync as a progressive extra where supported. Flush one conversation in order, but don't block other conversations behind a failing one. After 5 failed attempts or a 4xx (too long, blocked user), mark the message failed with 'Tap to retry' or 'Delete'. Attachments upload first to get an id, so the outbox row only holds that id. If the product didn't promise offline send, a memory queue plus a failed state would be acceptable.

deepDives.title: Many tabs: one socket and consistent unread counts
deepDives.problem: Three tabs each open a socket: three times the server connections, three copies of every event, and three tabs each sending read markers. Read a chat in one tab and the other two still show '5 unread' in their titles.

options.name: Socket per tab, sync state with BroadcastChannel
options.how: Every tab connects; tabs broadcast read changes to each other.
pros: Each tab is independent if another crashes
cons: N sockets per user
Every tab processes every event

options.name: Leader election with Web Locks plus BroadcastChannel
options.how: navigator.locks.request('chat-socket') is held by one tab; it owns the socket and relays events. When it closes, the lock passes to a waiting tab.
pros: Built-in failover, no heartbeat election code
cons: Leader tab may be throttled in the background
Relay adds a hop and serialisation cost

options.name: SharedWorker owns the socket
options.how: A SharedWorker holds the socket and store; tabs connect via MessagePort.
pros: Socket lives outside any tab's main thread
cons: Not available everywhere, notably Chrome for Android
Harder to debug

deepDives.choice: Web Locks leader plus BroadcastChannel, with a SharedWorker as an optional upgrade on desktop. Unread stays correct because it is derived (lastSeq − lastReadSeq), never incremented, so a replayed event can't double-count. Only mark read when document.visibilityState is visible, the window has focus and the message is on screen. Total unread goes into document.title and the favicon badge. Background tabs throttle timers, so the leader's ping uses the socket's own traffic plus a check on visibility change.

deepDives.title: Message list rendering
deepDives.problem: Chat lists are upside down compared to feeds: they open at the bottom, grow at the bottom, and load history at the top. Prepending 50 older messages must not move what the user is reading, and new messages should scroll the view only if the user is already at the bottom.

options.name: flex-direction: column-reverse
options.how: Let the browser treat the bottom as the start of the scroll container.
pros: Stays pinned to the bottom with no JavaScript
cons: Reading order and keyboard order are reversed unless the DOM is in reverse order too
Fiddly with virtualisation

options.name: Virtual list with bottom anchoring
options.how: Window ~40 bubbles; on prepend, add the height of the new items to scrollTop; on append, auto-scroll only if within 100 px of the bottom.
pros: Full control of 'jump to latest' and 'first unread' positions
cons: Variable heights (images, links) need measuring
Scroll correction bugs are visible

deepDives.choice: Virtual list with bottom anchoring. The list is role=log with aria-live=polite on a separate hidden region that announces only messages from others, one at a time, so a busy group doesn't flood the screen reader. When not at the bottom, show a 'N new messages · Jump' button instead of scrolling. Images reserve space from width and height in the payload. Keep focus in the composer after sending. For short histories (under ~300 messages) a plain list is fine.

failures: Server deploy drops 1 M sockets at once
Full-jitter backoff spreads reconnects over 30 s; the server can also send a close code with a suggested retry delay.
Ack is lost; the client resends
Server dedupes on (sender, clientId) and returns the original seq; client merges on clientId.
Sync cursor too old after a long weekend
Server answers 409 reset; client reloads conversation list and latest 50 messages for each open conversation, marks history above as 'load on scroll'.
Outbox rows are in IndexedDB; the new leader takes the lock and flushes them; dedupe makes the overlap harmless.
IndexedDB is unavailable or over quota
Fall back to memory with a visible 'messages may not survive a reload' notice; evict oldest cached history first, never the outbox.
Render as text nodes, linkify safely, sanitise any rich text with an allow-list, strict CSP; never trust server HTML.
scale: Huge groups (10 000 members): drop per-member read receipts, throttle typing indicators to one per 5 s, batch incoming messages per frame.
Many conversations (1 000+): page the conversation list, subscribe to live updates only for recent ones, and fetch others on open.
Heavy parsing (markdown, E2EE decrypt, search index): move it to a Web Worker so the main thread keeps a 16 ms frame.

followups.q: How do you test the reconnect logic?
answer: Make the state machine a pure function of (state, event) → (state, effects) and unit test each transition.
Use a fake socket and fake timers to simulate close, missed pong, offline, online and 4401.
Add an end-to-end test that kills the server mid-send and asserts one copy of each message.

followups.q: How do typing indicators work without flooding?
answer: Send 'typing' at most once per 3 s while keys are pressed; the server relays it.
Receivers hide the indicator 5 s after the last event; no 'stopped typing' event needed.
Never store them; they are fire-and-forget and skipped by sync.

followups.q: How do you support message edits and deletes?
answer: They are events with their own seq in the event stream, pointing at the message id.
The store updates the message in place; order doesn't change.
A deleted message keeps a tombstone so later edit events don't recreate it.

followups.q: How would you show notifications when the tab is in the background?
answer: Leader tab shows a Notification only if no tab is visible (ask the others over the channel).
When all tabs are closed, rely on Web Push through a service worker.
Collapse notifications per conversation with the tag option.

followups.q: Why not just poll every few seconds?
answer: At 1 M users and 3 s polling that is ~330 000 requests/s, nearly all empty.
Latency is up to 3 s; a socket is ~1 RTT.
Polling is a fine fallback when the socket is blocked, with a longer interval.

mistakes: Ordering messages by the client's clock.
Reconnecting immediately in onclose, with no backoff, no jitter and no offline state.
Keeping unread as a counter that gets incremented, so replays and multiple tabs double-count it.
Generating the message id on the server only, so the optimistic copy and the echo appear as two messages.
Holding the outbox in memory and losing messages on reload.

mid: Defined client and server frame types including ack with clientId
Showed a sent message optimistically with sending, sent and failed states
Loaded older history by paging up with a cursor
Kept focus in the composer and announced incoming messages politely
senior: Drew the reconnect state machine with offline and auth states and jittered backoff
Ordered by server seq, deduped by clientId, detected gaps and filled them
Put the outbox in IndexedDB and relied on server dedupe for exactly-once effect
Derived unread from lastSeq − lastReadSeq and synced it across tabs with BroadcastChannel
Described sync-after-reconnect with a cursor and a reset path
Virtualised the message list with bottom anchoring
staff: Did the reconnect-storm arithmetic and justified full jitter
Proposed one socket per browser via Web Locks leader election, with failover
Covered long offline gaps (don't replay a weekend) and storage quota handling
Planned a worker for heavy parsing or decryption and field metrics for send-to-ack latency
